intro:
**The Most High and the Pathway of Ease**

Al-Aʿlā, "The Most High," is the eighty-seventh chapter of the Qur'an, comprising 19 verses of early Makkan revelation. It opens with the soaring, beloved liturgical command: *“Exalt the name of your Lord, the Most High (*Sabbiḥi isma Rabbika al-Aʿlā*)!”* (87:1). In the devotional life of the Prophet Muḥammad ﷺ, Sūrah al-Aʿlā held a deeply cherished, sacred station: ʿĀ'ishah, ʿAbdullāh ibn ʿAbbās. Al-Nuʿmān ibn Bashīr reported in authentic collections (Ṣaḥīḥ Muslim 865 and Sunan Abī Dāwūd 1424) that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ loved this sūrah above all the shorter chapters, reciting it regularly in the first cycle of the Friday congregational prayer, during the two annual ʿĪd celebrations, and in the final *Witr* prayer of the night. In nineteen melodious, comforting verses, Sūrah al-Aʿlā reveals the fourfold stages of cosmic creation, promises the unlettered Prophet that he will never forget the divine revelation (*sa-nuqri'uka fa-lā tansā*), promises to ease his path toward ultimate ease (*wa-nuyassiruka li-l-yusrā*), and traces the golden thread of monotheism back to the ancient scrolls of Abraham and Moses.

**The Structural Symmetry and the Ancient Scrolls**

The architecture of Sūrah al-Aʿlā moves across three luminous movements:

1. The Fourfold Creativity of the Most High (1–5): Commands the glorification of the Lord: - Who created and proportioned (*khalaqa fa-sawwā*), - And Who determined measure and guided (*qaddara fa-hadā*), - And Who brought forth the green pasture (*akhraja al-marʿā*), - And then made it black stubble / dry chaff (*ghuthā'an aḥwā*).

2. The Prophetic Assurance and the Useful Reminder (6–13): Guarantees the preservation of the Qur'an in the Prophet's memory, pledges divine ease. Commands the distribution of guidance: *“So remind, if the reminder should benefit!”* It divides humanity into two psychological responses: - *The Soul with Awe*: *“He who fears [Allah] will be reminded.”* - *The Wretched*: *“But the most wretched one will avoid it—he who will enter the Great Fire, in which he will neither die nor live!”*

3. The Secret of Purification and the Scrolls of Old (14–19): Delivers the immortal formula of spiritual felicity in verses 14–15: *“Certainly he has succeeded who purifies himself (*qad aflaḥa man tazakkā*). Remembers the name of his Lord and prays!”* It indicts human short-sightedness: *“Nay, you prefer the life of this world, while the Hereafter is better and more enduring (*wa-l-ākhiratu khayrun wa-abqā*)!”* The chapter concludes by connecting this revelation to the primordial spiritual history of mankind: *“Indeed, this is in the former scriptures—the scriptures of Abraham and Moses (*Ṣuḥufi Ibrāhīma wa-Mūsā*)!”*

The tradition preserves the sūrah's place in the first teaching of Madinah. Al-Bukhārī recorded from al-Barāʾ ibn ʿĀzib that the first Companions to reach the city were Muṣʿab ibn ʿUmayr and Ibn Umm Maktum, who taught the Qur'an there, then ʿAmmār, Bilāl and Saʿd, then ʿUmar with twenty riders, and last of all the Prophet ﷺ himself — and al-Barāʾ added that the Prophet ﷺ did not arrive until he, al-Barāʾ, had already learned to recite "Glorify the Name of your Lord, the Most High" and sūrahs like it. This chapter was thus among the very first Qur'an the Anṣār received. The Two Ṣaḥīḥs preserve the Prophet's ﷺ own pairing of it in his word to Muʿādh — "Why did you not recite 'Glorify the Name of your Lord, the Most High,' 'By the sun and its brightness,' 'By the night when it envelops'?" — and Aḥmad recorded, through Ubayy ibn Kaʿb, Ibn ʿAbbās, ʿAbdur-Raḥmān ibn Abzā and ʿĀ'ishah, that he used to recite this sūrah alongside "Say, O you who disbelieve" and "Say, He is Allah, the One," ʿĀ'ishah adding the two seeking-refuge chapters to her version.

verses.1:
> Glorify the Name of your Lord, the Most High

**The Sūrah That Opens on the Glorification**

The sūrah begins not with a statement and not with an oath but with a command: glorify. The command is the sūrah's first word, and the first word is the command of the glorification of the Name of the Lord. The sūrah that takes its name from the Most High opens on the act of the glorification of the Most High, and the opening is the sūrah's way of placing the act of worship at the beginning of its speech. The Book opens some of its sūrahs on the oath, and it opens others on the command, and the command of the glorification is the command of the act that the sūrah will carry through its verses.

**The Manner of the Glorification**

The second reading of the verse, the reading that takes the Most High to qualify the Name, gives the command its manner, and the manner is the manner that the commentators record in two directions. The first direction is the direction of the separation: the glorification of the Name is the glorification that keeps the Name apart from every other thing, and the separation is what the command requires. The second direction is the direction of the revealed names: the glorification is the praise of God with the names that God has revealed. The revealed names are the names of the Book, and the Book names them in its standing verse: "Call upon Allah or call upon the Most Compassionate—whichever you call, He has the Most Beautiful Names" (17:110).

The verse drew an immediate response in the practice of the Prophet ﷺ. Aḥmad recorded from Ibn ʿAbbās that whenever the Messenger of Allah ﷺ recited this verse he said, "Glory to my Lord, the Most High" — the verse's own words turned back on the Lord they name — and Qatādah transmitted the same practice. It became the Companion's habit as well: Ibn Isḥāq al-Hamdanī reported that Ibn ʿAbbās said it whenever he recited the verse, just as he answered the closing question of the sūrah that asks "Is not He able to give life to the dead?" with "Glory to You, of course." The reciter of the Qur'an, on this showing, was never only a reciter. The Book's commands drew speech back out of him, and this verse's command drew the oldest formula of all: glory.

**The Place in the Prayer**

The tradition records the place of the sūrah's verse in the prayer, and the place is the place of the prostration. The report states that when the verse of the sūrah of the Human — "So glorify the Name of your Lord, the Greatest" (56:74) — was revealed, the Prophet ﷺ told his Companions to enact it in the bowing. When the verse of this sūrah was revealed, he told them to enact it in the prostration. The two verses are the two verses of the two positions, and the two formulas followed: the formula of the bowing is the glorification of the Greatest, and the formula of the prostration is the glorification of the Most High. The sūrah's verse is the verse of the prostration, and the prostration is the place where the worshipper is nearest to the Lord, and the formula of the place is the formula of the sūrah's command.
verses.2:
> Who created and ˹perfectly˺ fashioned ˹all˺

**The Reason of the Command**

The command of the first verse is followed by the reason of the command, and the reason is stated in the acts of the Lord. The sūrah does not say why the Lord is to be glorified in a word of doctrine; the sūrah states the acts, and the acts are the reason. The first act named is the act of the creation, and the creation is the act that stands under every other act, because every other act is the act on what has been created. The sūrah's glorification is the glorification by the acts, and the acts are the sūrah's content of the command. The structure of the sūrah's first movement is the structure of the command and its reason: the command in the first verse, the reason in the verses that follow. The reason is the reason of the creation and the fashioning and the ordaining and the guiding and the bringing forth and the withering.

**The Fashioning Without Flaw**

The tradition states the fashioning in the form of the report, and the report is the report of the first man. The report states that God fashioned the first human being after He breathed into him of His own spirit, and that He left him without irregularity, and the report is the report recorded in the standing form of the tafsīr. The Book states the breath in its own standing verses: "So when I have fashioned him and had a spirit of My Own ˹creation˺ breathed into him, fall down in prostration to him" (15:29), and "then He fashioned them and had a spirit of His Own ˹creation˺ breathed into them. And He gave you hearing, sight, and intellect" (32:9). The breath is the breath of the fashioning, and the fashioning is the act that leaves no flaw, and the leaving of no flaw is the sūrah's mark of the act.
verses.3:
> and Who ordained precisely and inspired accordingly

**The Second Pair of the Chain**

The sūrah's chain of the acts continues in this verse, and the verse carries the second pair of the chain. The first pair was the creation and the fashioning, the act of the existence and the act of the form, and the second pair is the ordaining and the guiding, the act of the measure and the act of the direction. The two pairs together are the four acts of the sūrah's first movement so far, and the four acts are the sūrah's statement of the work of the Lord in its stages. The sūrah's chain moves from the making of the thing to the ordering of the thing, and the ordering is the work that follows the making, because the made thing is not left without the order. The sūrah's verse is the second link of the chain after the first pair, and the link is the link of the measure and the direction.

**The Order Without Flaw**

The broader implication of the verse, as the tradition records it, is the statement of the order of the creation as a whole. The creation is as it should be, without imperfection or flaw, and the statement is the statement that the Book makes in its standing verse: "You will never see any imperfection in the creation of the Most Compassionate. So look again: do you see any flaws?" (67:3). The order of the sūrah's verse is the order of that statement, and the statement is the statement of the perfection of the created. The sūrah's chain of the acts is the chain that ends in this statement: the created is measured, the created is guided, and the created is without flaw. The sūrah's glorification is the glorification of the order, and the order is the sūrah's content of the act of the ordaining.

**The Measure Decreed Before the Making**

Mujāhid gave the guiding of this verse its breadth: He guided man to distress and happiness, he said, and He guided the cattle to their pastures — the guidance of the verse is the built-in direction of every created thing toward what it needs. The reading is the verse's own kin, for the Book puts the pair on Moses' lips before Pharaoh (20:50 — *“Our Lord is the One Who has given everything its ˹distinctive˺ form, then guided ˹it˺”*). And the measuring itself has its report: Muslim recorded from ʿAbdullāh ibn ʿAmr that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said that Allah ordained the measures of all creation fifty thousand years before He created the heavens and the earth, and His Throne was over the water. The ordaining of this verse is therefore not an afterthought of the making. It is older than the sky and the earth, and the guidance is the made thing meeting a plan written before either existed.
verses.4:
> and Who brings forth ˹green˺ pasture

**The Turn from the Human Being to the Earth**

The sūrah's chain of the acts turns in this verse from the human being to the earth. The first three verses of the chain were the verses of the human being: the creation of the man, the fashioning of the man, the ordaining and the guiding of the man. The fourth verse of the chain is the verse of the earth, and the earth is the earth that brings forth the pasture. The turn is the sūrah's way of stating the breadth of the work of the Lord, and the breadth is the breadth from the one kind of the created to the other kind. The Lord who created the man is the Lord who brings forth the green, and the sūrah's chain states the two works in the same sequence, and the sequence is the sūrah's statement that the one Lord does both. The turn is the sūrah's move from the person to the ground, and the ground is the ground that gives.

**The Earth That Gives**

The earth of the sūrah's verse is the earth in its season of the giving, and the giving is the giving of the green. The Book states the earth in this form in its standing verses: "You see the earth lifeless, but as soon as We send down rain upon it, it begins to stir ˹to life˺ and swell, producing every type of pleasant plant" (22:5). The earth is lifeless, and the earth is made to stir, and the stirring is the producing of the plant, and the producing is the sūrah's verse in the form of the Book's standing statement. The sūrah's verse is the sūrah's use of the standing form, and the use is the sūrah's way of placing its act of the chain in the Book's law of the earth.
verses.5:
> then reduces it to withered chaff

**The Second Face of the Season**

The sūrah's verse gives the second face of the work of the earth, and the second face is the face of the withering. The previous verse stated the bringing forth of the green, and this verse states the reducing of the green to the withered chaff, and the two verses together are the season in its two faces. The season is the season of the earth in the work of the Lord, and the work of the Lord is the work that brings the green and the work that turns the green to the stubble. The sūrah's two verses are the two verses of the season, and the season is the sūrah's statement of the power of the Lord over the living things of the earth. The turning is the work that follows the bringing forth, and the following is the sūrah's way of stating the season as the season that is complete in its two faces.

Ibn ʿAbbās read the verse's last words plainly: dried up and altered — the pasture that was green is first dry and then other than it was, and the same reading is carried by Mujāhid, Qatādah and Ibn Zayd. The double word matters. A pasture that merely dries has ended a season; a pasture that is altered has been changed by an act, and the act is the Lord's. The sūrah puts the withering in the same chain as the creating and the guiding, one more work of the same hand, so that the season's small death is never read as nature running on its own.

**The Season as the Sign**

The season of the sūrah is the sign of the return, and the sign is the sign that the Book states in its standing verses. The earth is lifeless, and the earth is made to stir. The stirring is the producing of the plant, and the producing is the work of the Lord in the earth: "You see the earth lifeless, but as soon as We send down rain upon it, it begins to stir ˹to life and swell, producing every type of pleasant plant" (22:5). The sūrah's season is the season of that standing form, and the standing form is the form of the return of the dead earth to the life.
verses.6:
> We will have you recite ˹the Quran, O Prophet,˺ so you will not forget ˹any of it˺

**The Turn to the Encouragement**

The sūrah's first movement is complete, and the sūrah turns now to its second movement, the movement of the encouragement. The turn is the sūrah's change from the acts of the Lord to the promise of the Lord to the Prophet ﷺ, and the change is the sūrah's way of moving from the statement to the address. The sūrah has stated the work of the Lord in the six acts of the chain, and the sūrah now addresses the one who carries the sūrah: the Prophet ﷺ. The encouragement is the encouragement of the promise, and the promise is the promise of the recitation. The sūrah's second movement is the movement of the promises, and the promises run from this verse to the eighth, where the promise of the ease closes the movement. The verse is the first verse of the second movement, and the verse is the first promise.

**The Counsel Against the Hastening**

The Book states the counsel against the hastening in its standing verses, and the counsel is the counsel that the sūrah's promise follows. "Do not rush to recite ˹a revelation of˺ the Quran ˹O Prophet˺ before it is ˹properly conveyed to you, and pray, 'My Lord! Increase me in knowledge'" (20:114). "Do not rush your tongue trying to memorize ˹a revelation of˺ the Quran. It is certainly upon Us to ˹make you˺ memorize and recite it" (75:16–17). The counsel is the counsel of the waiting, and the waiting is the waiting for the proper conveyance of the revelation. The sūrah's promise is the promise that the counsel assumes: the memorizing and the reciting are the work of the Lord, and the work is what the sūrah's verse promises. The counsel and the promise are the two sides of the one doctrine, and the doctrine is the teaching about the recitation as the work of the Lord.
verses.7:
> unless Allah wills otherwise. He surely knows what is open and what is hidden

**The Abrogation**

The sūrah's exception is the exception of the abrogation, and the abrogation is the doctrine that the Book states in its standing verse. "If We ever abrogate a verse or cause it to be forgotten, We replace it with a better or similar one. Do you not know that Allah is Most Capable of everything?" (2:106). The standing verse states the two acts of the abrogation: the abrogation of the verse and the causing of the forgetting, and the standing verse states the two together with the replacement, and the replacement is the better or the similar. The sūrah's exception is the exception of that doctrine, and the doctrine is the doctrine that the sūrah's promise assumes. The sūrah's verse is the sūrah's use of the standing doctrine, and the use is the sūrah's way of placing its exception in the Book's law. The abrogation is the sūrah's ground, and the ground is what the sūrah's exception rests on.

**The Exception of the Will**

The promise of the previous verse carries its exception in this verse, and the exception is the exception of the will. The sūrah's promise was the promise of the no-forgetting, and the sūrah's exception is the exception that the forgetting, if it comes, comes by the will of the Lord rather than by the fault of the one who receives. The sūrah's statement is the statement of the relation of the promise to the will: the promise stands, and the will stands over the promise, and the will is the power that the sūrah's promise assumes. The exception is not the breaking of the promise; the exception is the statement of the ground of the promise, and the ground is the will of the Lord. The sūrah's verse is the sūrah's way of placing the promise under the will, and the placing is the sūrah's statement of the order of the two.

**The Forgetting as the Willing**

The tradition states the verse in the form of the answer to a thought, and the thought is the thought of the fault. The answer is the answer recorded in the standing form of the tafsīr, and the answer is the sūrah's way of removing the thought of the fault.

Qatādah closed the thought in one sentence: the Prophet ﷺ did not forget anything except what Allah willed. The sentence holds the promise and its exception in their exact proportions — the forgetting is never an accident of memory, never a lapse the bearer of the Book has to answer for; it is an act of the same will that made the promise. On this reading the exception is itself a comfort: whatever was set aside was set aside deliberately, by the One who knows what is open and what is hidden, and nothing of trust was ever lost.
verses.8:
> We will facilitate for you the Way of Ease

**The Reading of the Law**

The first reading of the verse, recorded in the tradition, takes the ease to be the ease of the law, and the ease of the law is the uncomplicated nature of the revealed law. The reading borrows its ground from the Book's standing statement of the ease of the law: "Allah intends ease for you, not hardship, so that you may complete the prescribed period and proclaim the greatness of Allah for guiding you, and perhaps you will be grateful" (2:185). The standing statement is the statement of the character of the law, and the character is the ease rather than the hardship. The reading takes the sūrah's verse to be the promise of that character to the Prophet ﷺ, and the promise is the promise that the law that will be revealed is the law of the ease. This first reading states the ease in the form of the law, and the law is the ease.

**The Reading of the Memory**

The second reading of the verse takes the ease to be the ease of the memory, and the reading is the reading that follows from the context of the two previous verses. The context is the context of the recitation and the no-forgetting, and the reading takes the sūrah's verse to be the promise that the Lord will make the memorizing of the Quran easy for the Prophet ﷺ. That reading is the reading of the tafsīr recorded in the standing form, and it is the reading that the context favors. The sūrah's verse is the verse of the ease in the form of the memory, and the memory is the ease that the two previous verses promise. The reading is the reading of the character of the work of the Lord in the man, and the character is the ease.

**The Reading of the Paradise**

The third reading of the verse takes the ease to be the ease of the way into the Paradise, and the reading is the reading of the end. The reading takes the sūrah's verse to be the promise that the Lord will ease the way of the believers into the Paradise, and the promise is the promise of the ease at the end of the journey. The third reading is recorded in the standing form of the tafsīr, and it is the reading that moves the ease from the world of the revelation to the world of the reward. The sūrah's verse is the verse of the ease in the form of the way, and the way is the way into the Paradise. The reading is the reading of the ease in its further scope, and the scope is the scope of the end of the journey.
verses.9:
> So ˹always˺ remind ˹with the Quran˺—˹even˺ if the reminder is beneficial ˹only to some˺

**The Command After the Promise**

The sūrah's second movement is complete, and the sūrah turns now to its command. The command is the command of the reminder, and the command is the sūrah's instruction to the Prophet ﷺ that follows the promises. The sūrah's structure is the structure of the promise and the command: the promises are the promises of the Lord to the receiver of the message, and the command is the command of the Lord to the carrier of the message. The sūrah's turn is the sūrah's way of moving from the encouragement to the duty, and the duty is the duty of the reminder. The sūrah's command is the command that the promises lead to: the Lord promises the recitation and the no-forgetting and the ease, and the Lord commands the reminder. The command is the sūrah's third movement, and the movement begins with this verse.

**The Form of the Command**

The form of the command is the form of the imperative, and the imperative is the sūrah's way of stating the duty. The sūrah does not describe the reminder; the sūrah commands it, and the command is the command of the act that the Prophet ﷺ is to do. The imperative of the sūrah is the imperative of the Book at its moments of the instruction, and the instruction is the instruction of the carrier of the message. The sūrah's command is the command of the reminder with the Quran, and the reminder is the reminder that the sūrah's title states: the reminder is the sūrah's work. The sūrah's form is the form of the command, and the command is the sūrah's way of placing the duty on the one who carries the message.

**ʿAlī's Rule for Teaching**

Ibn Kathir draws the etiquette of knowledge straight from this verse: remind where reminding benefits, and do not waste the reminder on those not fit to receive it. The Commander of the believers ʿAlī ibn Abī Ṭālib is recorded saying, "You do not tell people any statement that their intellects do not grasp except that it becomes a trial for some of them," and again, "Tell people what they know — would you like Allah and His Messenger to be rejected?" The two sayings are the verse turned into method. The reminder profits the one who fears, so the reminder is paced to the listener, not to the speaker's store of learning; the sūrah's next verses give the reason, for the awe that receives the reminder is God's work in a heart, and the teacher's task is to meet that work, not to force it.
verses.10:
> Those in awe ˹of Allah˺ will be mindful ˹of it˺

**The First Class Named**

The sūrah's third movement begins with the naming of the first class, and the first class is the class that hearkens to the reminder. The sūrah's contrast is the contrast of the two classes, and the two classes are the class that hearkens and the class that shuns, and the sūrah names the first in this verse. The naming of the first class is the sūrah's way of opening the contrast, and the contrast is the sūrah's statement of the two receptions of the reminder. The sūrah's command of the previous verse was the command of the reminder, and the sūrah now states the one to whom the reminder is the reminder: the one who is in awe of the Lord. The sūrah's first class is the class of the awe, and the awe is the condition of the hearkening.

**The Word of the Awe**

The word the sūrah gives the first class is the word for the awe, and the awe is the state of the one who holds the threat of the Lord in the heart. The tradition records the word in the two directions of the certainty: the one who is certain of the return to God, and the one who admits the return but is not certain of it, are the two of the class of the awe. The two directions are the two degrees of the certainty, and the two degrees are what the tradition records of the state. The Book states the form in its standing verse: "So remind with the Quran ˹only˺ those who fear My warning" (50:45).
verses.11:
> But it will be shunned by the most wretched

**The Second Class Named**

Here the contrast turns to its second class, and the second class is the class that shuns the reminder. The sūrah's first class was the class that hearkens, and the sūrah's second class is the class that shuns, and the two classes are the two of the sūrah's third movement. The naming of the second class is the sūrah's way of completing the contrast, and the contrast is the sūrah's statement of the two receptions of the reminder. The sūrah's command of the reminder is the command that the two classes receive in their different ways, and the different ways are the hearkening and the shunning. The verse names the second class, and the naming is the naming of the class by its mark, and the mark is the word for the wretched.

**The Word for the Wretched**

The word the sūrah gives the second class is the word for the most wretched, and the wretchedness is the state of the one who has turned from the reminder. The tradition records the word in the form of the denial: the most wretched is the one who denies the return to God, and the denying is the state that separates the second class from the first. The first class held the return in the heart, and the second class denies the return, and the denying is the mark of the wretchedness. The contrast of the sūrah is, in the end, the contrast of the two states, and the two states are the holding and the denying. The sūrah's word of the wretched is the sūrah's way of naming the second class by its state, and the state is the state of the denial of the return.
verses.12:
> who will burn in the greatest Fire

**The Consequence Stated**

The sūrah's statement of the second class reaches its consequence in this verse, and the consequence is the consequence of the shunning. The sūrah's second class shuns the reminder, and the sūrah now states the end of the shunning: the end is the fire. Here the contrast moves from the naming of the class to the statement of the consequence, and the consequence is the statement of the end of the state. The verse closes the statement of the second class so far, and the closing is the closing in the form of the fire. The sūrah's contrast is the contrast of the two ends: the end of the first class and the end of the second, and the end of the second is stated in this verse.

**The Standing Form of the Fire**

The Book states the fire of the end in its standing verses, and the standing form is the form of the statement that the fire is the fire of the end of the evildoer. "Whoever comes to their Lord as an evildoer will certainly have Hell, where they can neither live nor die" (20:74). "It does not let anyone live or die, scorching the skin" (74:28–29). The standing form is the form of the statement that the fire of the end is the fire that the evildoer meets, and the meeting is the meeting of the end. The sūrah's verse is the sūrah's use of the standing form, and the use is the sūrah's way of placing its consequence in the Book's law.
verses.13:
> where they will not ˹be able to˺ live or die

**The Meaning of the State**

The tradition records the meaning of the state in the form of the phrase, and the phrase is the phrase of the Arabic at its moments of the great trial. The saying that one neither lives nor dies is the saying that the one is in the state of the great trial, and the trial is the trial that is between the two states. The meaning of the state is the meaning of the suffering that does not end in the rest of the death and does not continue in the life of the world. The sūrah's state is the state of that meaning, and the meaning is the meaning that the tradition records. "Whoever comes to their Lord as an evildoer will certainly have Hell, where they can neither live nor die" (20:74). "It does not let anyone live or die, scorching the skin" (74:28–29).

**The State Within the Fire**

The sūrah's consequence of the second class completes itself in this verse, and the completion is the completion in the form of the state. The previous verse stated the fire, and this verse states the state of the one who is in the fire, and the state is the state of the neither-life-nor-death. The sūrah's two verses of the consequence are the fire and the state, and the two together are the consequence in its complete form. The sūrah's statement is the statement of the relation of the fire to the state: the fire is the place, and the state is the condition of the one in the place, and the two are the place and the condition. The verse closes the statement of the second class, and the closing is the closing in the form of the state.

**The Form of the Neither**

The form of the verse is the form of the neither, and the neither is the form of the state that is between the two. The one in the fire is not in the state of the life, and the one in the fire is not in the state of the death, and the two negations together are the state. The Book states the form in its standing verses: "As for the disbelievers, they will have the Fire of Hell, where they will not be ˹allowed to be˺ finished by death, nor will its torment be lightened for them" (35:36).

**The Group That Dies in the Fire**

The state of neither dying nor living has its report. Aḥmad recorded from Abū Saʿīd al-Khudrī that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said that the people of the Fire who are its people will neither die nor live; but a people Allah wants mercy for He will cause to die in the Fire — they burn by their sins until they are like coal — and then intercession will be permitted. They will be brought group after group and scattered on the rivers of Paradise, and it will be said, "O people of Paradise, pour down upon them," and they will sprout like the seed on the bank of a stream in flood. Muslim recorded the report as well. The Prophet ﷺ then asked his hearers whether they had not seen the tree that is green, then yellow, then green again — and one of those present said, "It is as if the Messenger of Allah ﷺ used to live in the desert wilderness," so natural were the images he taught with. The report gives the terrible phrase of this verse its exact scope: the neither-nor is the lot of those who are the Fire's own, while for the others the death in the Fire is the doorway back to the rivers.
verses.14:
> Successful indeed are those who purify themselves

**The Word of the Prosperity**

The word the sūrah gives the consequence of the first class is the word for the prosperity, and the prosperity is the state of the one who succeeds. The sūrah's statement is the statement of the relation of the hearkening to the prosperity: the hearkening is the act of this world, and the prosperity is the state of the world to come, and the two are the act and its consequence. The sūrah's word of the prosperity is the word of the Book at its standing moments of the success, and the standing form is the form of the statement that the one who succeeds is the one who does the act that the Book commands. The sūrah's verse is the sūrah's use of the standing form, and the use is the sūrah's way of naming the consequence of the first class in the Book's law.

**The Purification**

The act that the sūrah gives the prosperous class is the act of the purification, and the purification is the act that the sūrah's next verse will complete with the remembrance and the prayer. The tradition records the purification in the three readings, and the three readings are the three objects of the act. The first reading takes the purification to be the purification from the idolatry by the profession of the oneness of God, and the reading is the reading of the purification from the false. The second reading takes the purification to be the purification through the good deeds, and the reading is the reading of the purification by the act.
verses.15:
> remember the Name of their Lord, and pray

**The Completion of the Acts**

The sūrah's statement of the first class completes itself in this verse, and the completion is the completion of the three acts. The previous verse stated the first act, the purification, and this verse states the second and the third, the remembrance and the prayer. The three acts together are the worship of the one who is prosperous, and the worship is the worship of the heart and the tongue and the body. The sūrah's two verses are the two verses of the consequence of the first class, and the two together are the consequence in its complete form. The sūrah's contrast is the contrast of the two classes in their consequences, and the consequence of the first class is now stated in its complete form. The sūrah's verse is the sūrah's way of closing the statement of the first class, and the closing is the closing in the form of the three acts.

**The Verse of the Zakāt al-Fiṭr**

The tradition tied this verse and the one before it to the charity that closes the fast. The Commander of the believers ʿUmar ibn ʿAbd al-ʿAzīz used to command the people to give the ṣadaqat al-fiṭr and would recite these two verses — success to the one who purifies himself, remembers his Lord and prays. Abū al-Aḥwaṣ drew the practical rule: if a beggar comes to any of you and the time for prayer arrives, he said, give him the charity first and then pray, because of this very verse. Qatādah gave the engine of the reading: he purifies his wealth and pleases his Creator. On this line of reading the purification of the verse is not only the soul's — the wealth is washed with it, and the feast-day charity is the washing made public.
verses.16:
> But you ˹deniers only˺ prefer the life of this world

**The Turn to the Rebuke**

The sūrah's third movement is complete, and the sūrah turns now to its fourth movement, the movement of the rebuke. The rebuke is the rebuke of the preference, and the preference is the preference of the world over the end. The sūrah's contrast stated the two classes and their consequences, and the sūrah now states the root of the preference of the second class, and the root is the preference of the world. The sūrah's verse is the sūrah's way of opening the rebuke, and the opening is the opening in the form of the address. The sūrah's turn is the sūrah's way of moving from the contrast to the rebuke, and the rebuke is the sūrah's fourth movement.

**The World as the Object**

The object of the preference is the life of the world, and the world is the world in its life. The sūrah's naming of the world is the naming of the world in its appeal, and the appeal is the appeal of the life of the world. The tradition records the state of the world in the form of the report, and the report is the report of the relation of the world to the two classes: the world is the prison of the believer and the garden of the disbeliever. The report is the report recorded in the standing form of the hadith, and the report states the two states of the world in the two classes. The world is the object of the preference, and the preference is the sūrah's mark of the second class.
verses.17:
> even though the Hereafter is far better and more lasting

**The Two Marks of the End**

The verse gives the end its two marks, and the two marks are the better and the more lasting. The first mark is the mark of the quality: the end is better than the world, and the better is the quality of the end over the world. The second mark is the mark of the duration: the end is more lasting than the world, and the more lasting is the duration of the end over the world. The two marks together are the sūrah's statement of the end in its relation to the world, and the relation is the relation of the better and the more lasting. The verse states the two marks, and the two marks are the sūrah's ground of the refusal.

**The Contrast of the Durable**

The sūrah's contrast in this verse is the contrast of the durable and the passing, and the passing is the world and the durable is the end. The sūrah's statement is the statement of the relation of the two: the world is the passing, and the end is the durable, and the one who prefers the passing over the durable is the one whom the sūrah rebukes. The sūrah's rebuke is the rebuke of the choice of the passing, and the choice is the choice that the sūrah's previous verse named. The sūrah's verse is the sūrah's statement of the durable, and the durable is the sūrah's ground of the refusal. The contrast of the two is the sūrah's argument of the rebuke, and the argument is the argument of the durable over the passing.

**The Two Loves**

Aḥmad alone recorded the report of Abū Mūsā al-Ashʿarī that draws this verse's line in one sentence: the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said that whoever loves his worldly life harms his Hereafter, and whoever loves his Hereafter harms his worldly life — so prefer what remains over what perishes. The report is the verse's arithmetic in the imperative: two loves, each taxing the other, and the believer is told which one to keep. Ibn Kathir's gloss on the verse runs along the same line — the world is lowly and temporal, the Hereafter noble and eternal, and an intelligent person does not trade the eternal for the soon-to-vanish. The rebuke of the previous verse is thus not a command to renounce the world but a command to weigh it, and the weighing has only one honest outcome.
verses.18:
> This is certainly ˹mentioned˺ in the earlier Scriptures—

**The Turn to the Connection**

The sūrah's fourth movement is complete, and the sūrah turns now to its fifth movement, the movement of the connection. The connection is the connection of the sūrah to the earlier scriptures, and the earlier scriptures are the scriptures that came before. The sūrah's statement is the statement that what the sūrah has stated is stated in the earlier scriptures, and the statement is the sūrah's way of placing its content in the line of the revelation. The verse opens the connection, and the opening is the opening in the form of the affirmation. The sūrah's turn is the sūrah's way of moving from the rebuke to the connection, and the connection is the sūrah's fifth movement.

**The Affirmation**

The form of the verse is the form of the affirmation, and the affirmation is the sūrah's way of stating the connection in the certain form. The sūrah does not suggest that the content of the sūrah is in the earlier scriptures; the sūrah affirms it, and the affirmation is the affirmation of the certainty. The sūrah's word of the affirmation is the word of the Book at its standing moments of the connection, and the standing form is the form of the statement that the content of the revelation is the content of the line. The Book states the form in its standing verse: "And it has indeed been ˹foretold˺ in the Scriptures of those before" (26:196). The sūrah's verse is the sūrah's use of the standing form, and the use is the sūrah's way of stating the connection in the Book's law.

Ibn Jarīr preferred to read "this" as pointing at the whole preceding discourse — the purification, the remembrance and the prayer, the preference of the Hereafter over the world — so that the verse's claim is that this teaching, item by item, is what the former scriptures carried; he calls the reading good and strong, and Qatādah and Ibn Zayd are reported with something like it. Abū al-ʿĀliyah compressed it further: the story of this sūrah is in the earlier scriptures. The readings agree on what matters. The sūrah is not claiming to quote the scrolls; it is claiming continuity with them, and the claim is checkable in principle — anyone holding the old books can test whether success through purification, prayer and the preference of the end was ever taught anywhere else.
verses.19:
> the Scriptures of Abraham and Moses

**The Two Scriptures Named**

The sūrah's connection completes itself in this verse, and the completion is the completion in the form of the naming. The previous verse affirmed the connection to the earlier scriptures, and this verse names the earlier scriptures in their two: the scriptures of Abraham and the scriptures of Moses. The sūrah's two verses of the connection are the affirmation and the naming, and the two together are the connection in its complete form. The sūrah's naming is the naming of the two of the line, and the two are the two whom the sūrah states as the holders of the earlier scriptures. The sūrah's verse is the sūrah's way of closing the connection, and the closing is the closing in the form of the naming.

**The Two of the Line**

The two named are the two of the line of the revelation, and the line is the line from the first to the last. The sūrah's statement is the statement that the content of the sūrah is the content of the two, and the two are the two of the line that the sūrah's affirmation assumed. The sūrah's verse is the sūrah's way of placing its content in the line of the two, and the line is the line of the revelation. The sūrah's naming of the two is the sūrah's statement of the unity of the content in the line, and the unity is the unity of the revelation.

**The Parallel in the Star Sūrah**

The Book itself states the contents of the scrolls at their closest, in the passage of the Star that names the scriptures of Moses and Abraham (53:36–42). The items match this sūrah point for point: "˹They state˺ that no soul burdened with sin will bear the burden of another" (53:38), "and that each person will only have what they endeavoured towards" (53:39) — and after those, that the deeds will be seen, that the recompense will be full, and that the ending is the return to the Lord. Purification, accountability, effort, return: the teaching of this sūrah is the teaching the Book attributes to the oldest scriptures, and the sūrah's last verse names the two carriers so that the listener knows the line runs from Abraham and Moses to the reciter of this page without a break.
